**Status: Phase 0 delivered (2026.01-rc1).** The [research paper](#paper) records the design; a shipped, gate-verified Phase 0 stands behind it. The [TR-14 exit PR](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/pull/108) carries the exit checklist with per-criterion evidence. What exists on `main` today, per component:

- **Kernel shield** — a CO-RE XDP shield (ACL, verdict cache, ban table) plus a TC flow producer and Go loaders ([shield loaders, merge ed9b271](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/commit/ed9b2714512ecad1bb6b0960eeeb7951e9693726)). The in-VM kernel enforcement E2E shows four facts ([#10](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/10#issuecomment-6093609582)): the ban `TC_ACT_SHOT`; the expiry auto-lift; the reconciler; the JSONL evidence.
- **Userspace engine, ladder slices** — a transparent proxy behind NGF with hop evidence ([#6](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/6#issuecomment-6091479891)); ingest → HTTP/1 parse → ladder S0–S5 with the verdict vocabulary. The slices:
  - **CEL** rule env carrying the request view
  - **CRS** via embedded Coraza — the CI-blocking parity gate reads **19/19, 100% verdict parity** ([#7](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/7#issuecomment-6092716820))
  - **bot fingerprints** — JA4 + headers v0 ([#99](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/pull/99))
  - **positive security** — the OpenAPI 3.1-subset gate on the demo route ([#13](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/13#issuecomment-6092602177))
  - the **rate-ban shadow** — ScoredWindowBan v1 with evidence records and kernel-enforced E2E ([#95](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/pull/95), [#105](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/pull/105))
- **Operator compile→load** — the `WAFPolicy` CRD compiles to Bundle v1 (fail closed) and hot-reloads the engine. The sealed in-process round-trip test runs in 0.239 s ([#98](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/pull/98)). The live apply→effect M9 run measures 2618 ms within the 5 s budget ([#76](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/76#issuecomment-6093110531)).
- **OTel verdict triad** — a trace span, the `verdicts_total` metric and a structured log, correlated by request id ([#11](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/11#issuecomment-6092518259)).
- **The DX1 lab** — a one-command demo: `bash lab/demo.sh` (setup → timed apply→effect → hop evidence) ([building](building.html)).

**Honest non-claims** (named, not hidden): the **<10 ms inline benchmark is pending [TR-24](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/24)**. The harness does not exist yet. The engine ladder does not yet serve in-cluster on live ringbuf traffic (**TR-15**). HTTP/2+gRPC and the h2/h3 posture are **TR-25/TR-29**. Production OTLP wire-out is not wired. The full exit-criteria table with every evidence link lives in the repo [README](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula#readme). This is research for adoption — not a product pitch.
:::

## What Trishula is — concretely

Trishula is a web application and API firewall for Kubernetes. The install is three Kubernetes workloads, driven by Helm and `kubectl apply`:

1. **`trishula-shield`** — a DaemonSet. It attaches eBPF programs at two kernel altitudes:
   - **XDP** on every node's NIC — drops L3/L4 abuse at ~µs cost: IP ACLs, SYN/UDP-flood tarpits, repeat-offender bans, cached verdicts
   - **TC** on engine-node interfaces — flow classification, rate counters, the event stream to the engine
2. **`trishula-engine`** — a Deployment the gateway steers protected routes through (a plain Service behind an `HTTPRoute`). It runs the full HTTP inspection ladder in userspace:
   - **OWASP CRS** via embedded Coraza
   - developer-written **CEL rules**
   - **OpenAPI positive security** — it blocks anything a route's schema does not declare; it learns undeclared behaviour instead of blocking it
   - **JA4 + header + behavioural bot detection**
   - **per-route rate limits**
   - a scored **temporary-ban engine** (fail2ban's findtime/threshold/bantime model, re-specified for HTTP and kernel-enforced)
3. **`trishula-operator`** — a Deployment. It watches the four CRDs (`WAFPolicy`, `APISpec`, `RuleSet`, `BanPolicy`) and compiles them into signed bundles. The bundle carries: evaluator chains; a Vectorscan matcher DB for the hot regex subset; kernel map values; ban thresholds. The hot-reload budget is 5 s. Rollback re-pins the previous bundle and records the re-pin in the CRD.

**What a developer actually writes:** a CEL expression over a structured request view (`request.method == "POST" && path.matches("/v1/chat/*") && size(request.body.?json.messages) > 128`). They write the OpenAPI spec their API already has, plus the 4 YAML CRDs. No proprietary rule language, no vendor console, no sidecar config files.

**What it stops, specifically:**

- credential stuffing — auth-failure ratios + JA4 heterogeneity → scored bans
- request smuggling — strict normalization + a dedicated differential corpus
- slowloris and connection starvation — kernel flow counters, which per-request WAFs cannot see
- layered DoS on expensive AI endpoints — token-metered routes get per-route rate ladders + ban escalation
- prompt-injection-shaped payload abuse — an ML scorer cascade with an async judge
- known bot and tooling masquerades — JA4 + header order/entropy fingerprints against a digest-pinned tooling DB
- the OWASP Top-10 — CRS 4.x, with a CI-blocking verdict-parity gate

**What it does not do (v1):** the exclusions:
- no service mesh
- no secrets vault
- no endpoint picker
- no web console (the team's OTel backend is the console)
- no HTTP/3 claim yet ([TR-29](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/29))
 Performance numbers carry the "target" label until the benchmark plan ([TR-24](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/24)) measures them.

## Why this project

A web application firewall inspects HTTP traffic and decides: allow, block, rate-suppress or tag. It is also the last major security control without developer ubiquity. Three developments make the shift feasible now. Each alone is an optimisation; together they are an opening:

- **Gateway API consolidation.** Kubernetes ingress is standardising on the Gateway API. The edge is being re-plumbed, and the WAF's integration point is contested. Whatever attaches cleanly to the new standard defines the next decade of edge policy.
- **eBPF maturity.** Kernel-altitude packet processing is dependable, inspectable and CO-RE-portable. Enforcement no longer needs a middleware hop: the cheapest decisions run where the packet arrives.
- **Machine-generated traffic at the WAF's entrance.** Agents, scrapers and automated abuse arrive faster than hand-written signatures can follow. Their fingerprints resist imitation.

Negative signatures alone cannot carry this load: the good-traffic risk is too high, and hand maintenance is too slow. The project's premise is therefore positive security, fingerprinting and behaviour analysis, with signatures as one (important) stage among several.

## Objectives

1. **Adoptability as a first-class feature** — CRD-driven policy; per-route promotion gates (learn → shadow → enforce); verdict telemetry a developer reads directly. The people who own the application own its protection.
2. **Full detection stack at kernel altitude** — negative signatures, positive security, bot detection and behaviour bans. The enforcement point is eBPF; a middleware chain cannot hold that position.
3. **Parity before novelty** — OWASP CRS runs via embedded Coraza as the reference evaluator; a CI-blocking differential suite verifies the engine matches it.
4. **Honest engineering** — fail-open defaults, evidence records for every ban, and exit criteria that report pass/fail as measured.

## How Trishula works

Trishula pairs a kernel-altitude eBPF shield with a full userspace detection ladder. The shape: three components, two planes, one decision record per request.

- **Shield** (DaemonSet, XDP/TC): ACL, verdict cache and ban table, enforced where the packet arrives; fail-open by default.
- **Engine** (Deployment): the detection ladder S0–S6 — CEL rules under cost budgets, OWASP CRS via embedded Coraza, OpenAPI positive security, rate limits, JA4/behavioural bot detection.
- **Operator** (Deployment): reconciles `WAFPolicy`/`BanPolicy` CRs into compiled engine bundles and pre-seeds the shield maps. Rollback is a CRD-recorded re-pin.

Each verdict is a correlated OpenTelemetry record (`trishula.verdict.v1`); dashboards ship in-repo.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    subgraph KERNEL["kernel plane"]
        xdp["eBPF shield<br/>XDP + TC"]
        maps["maps<br/>ACL · verdict cache · ban table"]
    end
    subgraph USER["userspace plane"]
        lad["detection ladder<br/>S0-S6"]
    end
    gw["Gateway API<br/>(NGF reference)"] --> lad
    lad --> app["app pods"]
    xdp --- maps
    lad -- verdicts --> otel[("OTLP<br/>trishula.verdict.v1")]
```

## Deployment model

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    subgraph cluster["Kubernetes cluster"]
        subgraph gwplane["gateway plane"]
            ngf["NGF (Gateway API)"]
        end
        subgraph wafplane["Trishula"]
            eng["engine deployment<br/>(plain backend Service)"]
            opr["operator<br/>(WAFPolicy / BanPolicy CRDs)"]
            sh["shield DaemonSet<br/>(XDP/TC eBPF)"]
        end
        app["application pods"]
    end
    clients["clients"] --> ngf
    ngf -- HTTPRoute --> eng
    eng --> sh
    eng --> app
    opr -- bundles + map pre-seed --> eng
    opr -- pinned maps --> sh
```

- **Install order:** operator → shield (DaemonSet) → engine. The operator reconciles `WAFPolicy` / `BanPolicy` CRs into compiled engine bundles (double-buffered) and pre-seeds the shield maps.
- **Gateway API integration:** the gateway steers to the engine as a plain backend (HTTPRoute); [NGF](https://github.com/nginx/nginx-gateway-fabric) is the reference data plane. The whole reference stack is OSS. Conformant alternatives (Envoy Gateway, Istio, Traefik, Emissary, kgateway) attach the same way. An `ext_proc` wire-contract variant for Envoy-family estates is feature-gated for later.
- **Fail-open by default:** an inline shaper must never become the outage; `failureMode` is explicit and audited per policy.
- **Rollback:** a CRD-recorded re-pin of the previous bundle — never a manual intervention.
- **Node requirements:** kernel ≥ 5.8; the shield is CO-RE and verifier-checked in CI.
- **Telemetry:** every verdict is an OTLP span + metric + log on `trishula.verdict.v1`; dashboards ship in-repo.

**Detection ladder** (short-circuit ordered): S0 kernel pre-clear (ACL, verdict cache, ban table) → S1 cache re-check → S2 CEL rules (cost-budgeted) → S3 OWASP CRS via embedded Coraza → S4 OpenAPI positive security → S5 rate limits → S6 bot fingerprints and behavioural windows.
ScoredWindowBan converts repeated abuse into kernel-enforced temporary bans. The bans carry evidence records; prefix escalation stays off by default.

## Design rationale

- **eBPF (XDP first, TC alongside)** — the only mechanism carrying kernel-altitude, programmable and verifiable packet policy on stock Kubernetes nodes. CO-RE keeps builds portable. Enforcement runs where the packet arrives; a middleware chain cannot hold that position.
- **Gateway API + NGF as reference** — Gateway API is where Kubernetes ingress is consolidating; NGF keeps the whole reference deployment OSS and mirrors the topology operators already run. Envoy-family estates get the feature-gated `ext_proc` variant later; single-data-plane lock-in is a non-goal.
- **Embedded Coraza, not a rule-engine rewrite** — CRS compatibility is the adoption surface; embedding yields exact parity by construction. The differential suite keeps a from-scratch fast path honest when it arrives (a Vectorscan hot subset, behind a shadow gate).
- **CEL as the first-class DSL** — typed, cost-budgeted evaluation; Kubernetes-native ergonomics. The compile step gates on cost before load. A general regex DSL cannot bound evaluation cost.
- **OpenAPI positive security with promotion gates** — specs already exist in application repositories. The learn → shadow → enforce path makes adoption incremental, instead of a big-bang policy cutover.
- **ScoredWindowBan over naive counters** — fail2ban-style bans with an algorithmic scoring window, evidence per ban, prefix escalation off by default. Shared-egress false positives are the practical ban-tooling failure.

- **OpenTelemetry as the verdict contract** — every verdict is a correlated span + metric + log. Security that cannot show its work cannot gain developer adoption.
- **Fail-open by default** — an inline kernel shaper must never become the outage; `failureMode` is explicit and audited per policy.

## Education and adoption

Security technology spreads when adoption gets simpler, not when tooling grows more powerful. The precedents are consistent:

| Precedent | What was hard | What made adoption cross over |
|---|---|---|
| Let's Encrypt | PKI was an expert discipline; certs cost money and ops time | One command (`certbot`), automation, free certs — TLS went from 40% to 90%+ of the web |
| fail2ban | log analysis and blocking were manual sec-ops work | A single daemon watched logs and banned offenders automatically — behaviour blocking became normal |
| Caddy / nginx + cert-manager | TLS termination per-service was hand-configured | Convention-first configs made correct TLS the default path |
| OWASP CRS | WAF rules were vendor black boxes | An open, community-maintained rule set made signature quality inspectable and shared |
| Kubernetes Gateway API | every edge had its own config dialect | Standard CRDs made edge policy portable and reviewable like code |

Trishula targets the same shift for the WAF. The education programme is the adoption mechanism, not an afterthought:

- **Academy modules with runnable labs** ([TR-27](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/27), [TR-28](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/28)) — HTTP on the wire, TLS, headers, fingerprints, positive security. Each module is a hands-on lab against a live cluster.
- **The 15-minute gate** ([TR-23](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/23), metric M3) — clone → first enforced rule in ≤ 15 minutes, timed nightly in CI. A regression stops the release.
- **Copy-paste-first policy recipes** — every lab ships the exact YAML a developer would commit. No dashboards are needed to understand a rule.
- **Promotion gates as the adoption path** — learn → shadow → enforce is both a safety mechanism and the adoption journey: observe first, intervene second. Each stage has a lab.
- **Verdict telemetry a developer can read** — one correlated OTel record per request. The record schema (`trishula.verdict.v1`) is documented like an API, because it is one.
- **Honest exit criteria** — every release states what works and what does not (the README checklist pattern).

The audience is the application developer and platform engineer who already runs Kubernetes — not the WAF specialist. Documentation, labs and error messages read at that level first.

The research paper (*“Trishula: An eBPF-Native, Developer-First Web Application and API Firewall for Kubernetes”*) is the research companion to this site. It carries the adoptability thesis, the field survey and the adoption plan. The survey covers Coraza, ModSecurity, SafeLine, open-appsec, CrowdSec, fail2ban and the eBPF cousins, with the feature-coverage matrix.
A public link lands here when the paper is archived; until then it travels with the project docs.
